text: A film director is disposed of in the opening minutes, and the picture carries on without him. What follows belongs to people with no standing whatever, scraping along the margins of a South Korean city in 1983, and Lee Jang-ho lets their movement — loitering, running, improvising — carry a criticism that plain speech would have to say out loud. The film is funny, and the humour is not a softening: the joke and the accusation arrive in the same gesture. Ninety-seven minutes of farce with something colder underneath, handing its characters bursts of freedom it never pretends will outlast the reel. They own almost nothing, which is exactly why the picture can afford to be reckless with them. Korea's film archive keeps it among the hundred titles of the national cinema, an odd berth for a work this uninterested in dignity.

For decades the one audience barred from this film was the American one. James Blue shot the 1963 civil rights march on Washington for the United States Information Agency, whose films were made for viewers abroad; the Smith-Mundt Act kept them off domestic screens without a special act of Congress, and Congress did not open that door until 1990. The premise shapes all thirty-three minutes. A crowd cannot be assumed, it has to be introduced, its purpose spelled out for a viewer in another country with no stake in the argument — and the spelling out is done by a government describing pressure applied to itself. In 2008 the Library of Congress took it into the National Film Registry. Paid for by the state, withheld from its own citizens, then kept as their history.

Thirty-eight Augustas: a street, a storefront, a whole town in Montana, another in Maine. Scott Nixon sold goods for a living out of Augusta, Georgia, travelled constantly to do it, and somewhere in that routine began collecting his home city's name wherever the road produced one — camera in hand, a member of the Amateur Cinema League, an amateur in the old sense of doing it for love and on his own money. Sixteen silent minutes, no argument, no destination. The pleasure lies in the compulsion, and in everything that falls into frame around the target: the buildings next door, whatever happened to be passing, ordinary American blocks nobody had a reason to photograph on purpose. The National Film Registry holds it now, a peculiar and correct fate for a hobby that has outlived every practical reason anyone had for it.

The score is the one thing this film declines to care about. Twenty-four minutes, 1967, the first feature produced by NFL Films, and the decision built into it — that a game is worth watching apart from who won it — is the reason a piece of league publicity now sits in the National Film Registry. Once the outcome is set aside, the camera has to locate value elsewhere: in postures, in weather, in the seconds before a snap, in the gap between a play as drawn and a play as bodies actually perform it. John Hentz was arranging rather than reporting. There is no suspense here in the ordinary sense, since anyone watching in 1967 knew the results already; what replaces it is the sport as physical event, enlarged until a collision becomes something to look at rather than something to score.

A committee counting sick miners in three states hired a filmmaker instead of printing another report. Lee Dick delivered sixteen minutes in 1940, and the film does not behave the way advocacy usually behaves — the mines of Kansas, Missouri and Oklahoma, the illnesses that came with the work, the households attached to both, all handled with formal invention rather than plain instruction. Half its value now is accidental. The ground it photographs had been dug out and heaped up by extraction until the region stopped resembling anywhere people would choose, and that record sits in the frames whether or not the camera was pointing at it. The Tri-State Survey Committee wanted the working conditions changed. What survives is partly the landscape the argument was standing on.

Eighteen minutes of animation from 1947 that put the crucifixion, a lynching and Nazi Germany into a single argument. The aim was doctrinal: Christian teaching restated for a world that had just acquired the means to finish itself, human conflict condemned by way of its worst available examples. Frank Tashlin took the assignment. Animation is what makes the attempt possible at all — figures that are made rather than cast can carry Scripture and atrocity in one register, and nobody has to be hired to play Christ or a mob. Whether that is a solution or an evasion is the live question, and at this length the question never has time to cool. It is a sermon and does not pretend otherwise, addressed to viewers assumed to be frightened, which in 1947 was not a large assumption.

Lee Jong-se is a third-rate comedian who believes he is a genius, and what he actually wants is to direct. Two hours and seven minutes is a long stretch to spend with a man that wrong about himself, and the length is the wager: the delusion has to be lived in rather than punctured, sustained well past the point where a shorter comedy would call time. The problem Lee Myung-se set himself in 1989 is one of distance. Too close and the routine is only sad; too far and the man is only a fool. Between the two sits the difference between the act Lee Jong-se performs and the act he believes he is performing, and that difference is where the comedy lives. Korea's film archive counts it among a hundred national titles — a verdict its hero would have taken as vindication.

Conducting is the one musical job where the whole of the labour is gesture and the whole of the product is other people's sound. Antonia Brico had the training and the technique, and spent a career against a profession that did not want a woman on its podium. Jill Godmilow's film, made in 1974, sits with her while she describes it, and the method is plain to the point of exposure: a subject, a camera, and time enough for her to talk at length without being managed. The striking part is how much of the talk is craft rather than grievance — tempo, rehearsal, what an orchestra does when it is not persuaded — from someone granted too few chances to practise any of it. An hour, near enough, is brief for a life and long for an interview. The difference goes to her voice.

The same story twice, by the same woman: first the way she has told it before, then the way it actually goes. Twenty minutes, 1972, one speaker, one dress bought at real expense and never worn. The first account is practised — timed, shaped, delivered by someone who knows where it lands. The second gives up the shape. What Liane Brandon found is that the distance between the two versions is the entire subject: not the dress and not the money, but the work of turning something painful into an anecdote, and then the harder work of setting the anecdote down. Almost nothing else is in the film, and that scarcity is a decision rather than a limit. It asks twice, and the second answer does what the first was built to prevent.

The business ran like this: a man arrives in a town, announces a film, and charges the parents of every child who wants to be in it. Melton Barker worked that circuit for four decades, from the 1930s into the 1970s, shooting the same twenty-minute kidnapping story over and over — a well-to-do girl, a pair of hoodlums — with new local children in every place he stopped. What survives is less a film than a form, filled in again and again by towns that had no other reason to be photographed. The performances are whatever children who have never acted and never will again can supply. The interest is in the faces, the streets behind them, the haircuts of one particular year in one particular county. A single version sits in the National Film Registry, standing in for the whole travelling enterprise.

A giraffe hunt takes days, and most of those days are walking. John Marshall filmed four Ju/'hoansi men through one such hunt in the Kalahari, using footage gathered on the Smithsonian–Harvard Peabody expedition of 1952–53, and cut it to seventy-two minutes for release in 1957. The result is pulled between two things: a record of technique — tracking, patience, the reading of ground — and a story with four men in it, edited toward suspense the way a drama is. That tension is now the most instructive thing about the film, since the question of whether an ethnographer may shape other people's work into a narrative has not gone quiet in the decades since. What comes through the argument intact is the walking: the distance covered, the heat, the arithmetic of getting meat out of a desert.

In 1966 the National Board of Review placed a documentary about a politician's career among the ten best films of the year. An unusual verdict, and a measure of what audiences would sit still for. Bruce Herschensohn had eighty-five minutes and a subject too recent to be seen from any distance: John F. Kennedy's public career, assembled while the people who had voted for and against him were still the audience for it. The mode is commemorative, and commemoration is a form with rules of its own — the ordering of events, the weight assigned to a speech, the music that settles in advance how a piece of newsreel will land. Much of the interest now lies in watching those rules operate. It is a first draft of a legacy, put together before anyone could know which parts would hold.

Felicia Bragg was a high-school student in Watts when three UCLA film students asked her to narrate her own life. Twelve minutes, finished before the rebellions of 1965 and sold as an educational film — a category built to be shown in classrooms and then forgotten. Trevor Greenwood, Robert Dickson and Alan Gorg constructed the picture around her voice instead of a narrator's, and she annotates as it goes: her family, her school, her streets, what she hopes for and what she is already tired of. Filming the ordinary condition of a place is much harder than filming its crisis, and the crisis had not yet arrived for anyone in the frame. Universities still run it in documentary courses. Made by students, it went back to students, and the girl doing the talking is why it holds.

The women of Barrio Sonadora, in Guaynabo, go on strike against their husbands. Thirty-five minutes, 1956, made within DivEdCo's programme of films about modernization in Puerto Rico — and here the instrument is turned on the house rather than the field or the road. The move is sharper than it first sounds: a tactic borrowed from organized labour, applied to cooking and washing and the raising of children, in a form built to be argued over afterwards by audiences living where the camera had just been. Benjamín Doniger stages it closer to demonstration than melodrama. Modesta leads, the husbands are left to work out what has been done to their evenings, and the film's whole confidence rests on a village recognizing both sides of its own kitchen.
